profile.summary: VenusREM predicts how single or multiple amino acid substitutions change a protein's fitness, without being trained on any measurements of the protein in question. It takes three inputs for the wild-type protein: its amino acid sequence, a structure in PDB format, and a set of homologous sequences found by alignment. A pretrained language model turns the sequence and the local structure around each residue into per-residue logits, a separate module turns the alignment into evolutionary logits, and the two are combined into one fitness score per mutant. The authors report Spearman correlations on 217 assays of the ProteinGym substitution benchmark and also test the model on a VHH antibody and on phi29 DNA polymerase mutants made in the laboratory.
profile.summary_source_locator: paper: Abstract, Section 2.1 Model overview, Section 2.4.3.1; README: Zero-shot Prediction for Mutants

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The sequence and the structure of the wild-type protein are first turned into tokens. The sequence uses a vocabulary of the 20 standard amino acids plus five special characters. For each residue the local structure, defined as up to 40 neighbouring residues within 10 angstroms, is embedded by a pretrained geometric vector perceptron trained as a denoising autoencoder on 4,735,677 local-structure graphs from CATH43-S40, and the resulting 256-dimensional vector is mapped by K-means into a codebook of 2048 structure tokens. A BERT-style protein language model combines the two token streams through disentangled multihead cross-attention to produce native logits for each residue and amino acid type. In parallel, homologous sequences retrieved by alignment are converted into evolutionary logits by a module that needs no extra training. A mutant's fitness score compares the logits of the mutant residues with those of the wild type, mixing the native and evolutionary terms; the mixing weight is the script's alpha option, which defaults to 0.8.
sections.source_locator: paper: Sections 2.2.1.1, 2.2.1.2, 2.3.1, 2.3.2, 2.3.3; compute_fitness.py: argument definitions

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: VenusREM is a scoring pipeline rather than a single downloadable checkpoint. The pretrained weights it loads are frozen and live in a separate Hugging Face repository, AI4Protein/ProSST-2048, which the inference script loads by default; a result should name that revision as well as the commit of this repository. The repository's news list records later work under the same name: VenusREM2 reported at 0.556 on the ProteinGym substitution leaderboard through a separate VenusREM-Harness repository in September 2026, and an integration into VenusFactory2 in April 2026. Neither is described here as a checkpoint of its own. The score also depends on which homology search produced the alignment, since the repository offers prepared EVcouplings a2m files and ColabFold a3m files for ProteinGym and a Jackhmmer route for new proteins.

strengths.text: The homology part is added at scoring time and needs no training, so a new alignment can be swapped in without refitting anything.
Inference does not need a forward pass per mutated position: the authors say their input preparation avoids mutating each position according to the DMS data or applying mask operations.
The hardware bar for inference is low by the authors' own account: they recommend at least 10 GB of graphics memory, such as an RTX 3080, and they ran the work on four of those cards.
The authors tested the predictions outside high-throughput benchmarks, on 31 VHH antibody mutants from the literature and on ten phi29 DNA polymerase mutants they made and measured.

limitations.text: The code is released under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, a non-commercial no-derivatives licence. Commercial use and modified redistribution are not permitted by it.
A structure is required as well as a sequence. For a protein with no experimental structure the authors point to prediction servers, and warn that wet-lab work needs the best structure available.

profile.summary: VespaG predicts the effect of missense single amino acid substitutions in a protein from its sequence alone. It embeds the sequence with the protein language model ESM-2 and passes the per-residue embedding through a feed-forward network with one hidden layer of 256 units, which outputs a score for each of the 20 amino acids at each position. Because experimental variant data is scarce, the network was not trained on measurements: it was trained to reproduce the scores of the alignment-based predictor GEMME on 39 million variants of the human proteome. The authors report a mean Spearman correlation of 0.48 plus or minus 0.02 on the 217 assays of the ProteinGym substitution benchmark, and say the whole mutational landscape of a proteome can be predicted in under 30 minutes on a 12-core laptop with 16 GB of memory.
profile.summary_source_locator: paper: Abstract and Section 3; README: header paragraphs

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The input sequence is embedded by a frozen protein language model. The default is ESM-2, specifically esm2_t36_3B_UR50D as the README names it; the pretrained language models were used as is, without fine tuning. Each residue's embedding goes through a feed-forward network with one hidden layer, 256 hidden units and dropout of 0.2, which outputs a substitution score for every amino acid at that position. The training target was not experimental data. For about 5000 human proteins, homologous sequences were aligned with the MMseqs2-based strategy of ColabFold, GEMME was run on each alignment to produce a complete substitution matrix of size L by 20 with scores from minus 10 to 2, and the network was trained to map embeddings to those scores. The authors describe this as a student learning from an expert teacher, and compared the one-hidden-layer network against a linear regression, a two-layer network and a small convolutional network before settling on it.
sections.source_locator: paper: Sections 2.1, 2.2 Model specifications and 3; README: header and predict options; utils.py: DEFAULT_MODEL_PARAMETERS

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The weights ship inside the repository, not on a model hub. At the commit read here model_weights holds three files: v1/esm2.pt, v2/esm2.pt and v2/prott5.pt. The code sets the model version to v2 and loads model_weights/v2/<embedding type>.pt, with esm2 as the default embedding type, so a plain run uses v2/esm2.pt. The package version in pyproject.toml is 0.1.0. A result should therefore name the commit, the weight version folder and the embedding type, and also the language model used for the embeddings, since embeddings are either supplied by the user or generated at run time. What differs between v1 and v2 is not stated in the sources read. Retraining is possible: the repository drives it with DVC and offers precomputed embeddings and GEMME scores on Zenodo.

strengths.text: Fast and light once embeddings exist: the authors report predicting all mutational landscapes of a proteome in under 30 minutes on a 12-core laptop with 16 GB of memory.
Prediction needs no alignment at run time. The alignments were used only to make the GEMME training labels.

strengths.text: The authors say the setup is easily retrainable with a new or updated language model, and the repository ships a DVC pipeline plus Zenodo embeddings and GEMME scores so that retraining can be repeated.
The evaluation can be rerun from the repository: an eval subcommand downloads the ProteinGym reference and score files and computes Spearman correlation per assay.

limitations.text: GPL-3.0 is copyleft. Code that includes VespaG and is distributed must carry the same licence, which matters for closed products.

The predictions are only as good as the teacher: the labels are GEMME scores, not measurements, and the authors flagged landscapes built from fewer than a couple of hundred homologous sequences as low confidence.
The speed claim assumes the ESM-2 embeddings already exist. If none are supplied they are generated first, and the README warns that generating them on CPU can be slow.
The authors warn about the state of the codebase themselves: it began as a Bachelor's thesis and they say design choices were never fixed, although the project is still supported.
It scores missense single amino acid substitutions. The sources read describe no handling of insertions or deletions.

profile.summary: IntelliFold predicts the all-atom structure of a biomolecular complex from its sequences, in the manner of AlphaFold 3. The current release, IntelliFold-2, takes an AlphaFold 3 style JSON input listing the chains and ligands, runs a Pairformer trunk and a diffusion sampler, and writes predicted coordinates with confidence scores. The developers report it on FoldBench against AlphaFold 3, Boltz, Chai-1 and Protenix, with the gains concentrated in antibody-antigen interfaces and protein-ligand co-folding. Code and weights are Apache-2.0 and the weights are hosted on Hugging Face; a hosted server runs a further variant that is not released.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: header, Inference and License; release note: Introduction and Benchmark Performance

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: IntelliFold follows the AlphaFold 3 design: a Pairformer trunk over token representations feeding a diffusion module that generates all-atom coordinates. The release note describes what changed in version 2. The latent representations inside the Pairformer blocks were widened, which the authors say both raises capacity and improves hardware utilisation. The atom attention mechanism was reformulated for consistency between training and inference, and atom-level tokenisation is applied stochastically. The diffusion sampler was fine tuned with Proximal Policy Optimization, treating the sampler as a stochastic policy, which the authors say reduces unstable or low-quality trajectories. Training used a focal-loss style reweighting that puts more gradient on hard examples, and the Protein Data Bank was reprocessed with an updated pipeline alongside a larger self-distillation dataset. The release note calls PPO-enhanced sampling and the difficulty-aware loss exclusive to IntelliFold-2-Pro, the server-only variant, so the released IntelliFold-2 and IntelliFold-2-Flash weights do not include them. At inference an optional steering mode adds, at every denoising step, the gradient of a set of differentiable physical potentials covering bond lengths and angles, clashes, chirality, planarity, van der Waals overlap, covalent connections and symmetric chain repulsion.
sections.source_locator: release note: Key Technical Changes; README: Inference, steering paragraph; release note: model variants list

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three variants of version 2 exist, and only two are released. IntelliFold-2-Flash has 12 standard Pairformer blocks and is offered for academic use and fine tuning; IntelliFold-2 has 48 widened Pairformer blocks with latent space scaling and is the most accurate released model; IntelliFold-2-Pro adds PPO-enhanced sampling and difficulty-aware loss and runs only on the developers' server. The Hugging Face repository holds intellifold_v0.1.0.pt from the first release, intellifold_v2.pt, intellifold_v2_flash.pt, and the JAX conversion intellifold_v2.bin.zst with intellifold_v2_fourier.npz, at the revision read here. Since June 2026 the repository runs version 2 on the AlphaFold 3 JAX engine, vendored at version 3.0.3, and the JAX weights were converted from the PyTorch checkpoint with convert_ifv2_to_jax.py. A result should name the variant, the weight file, the engine and whether steering was on, because steering changes the sampler.

profile.summary: OpenFold3 is an open reproduction of AlphaFold 3 by the AlQuraishi Lab at Columbia University and the OpenFold consortium. It predicts the structure of a biomolecular complex from its sequences, covering standard and non-canonical protein, RNA and DNA chains together with small molecules, and it writes coordinates in mmCIF with per-sample confidence files. Unlike most reproductions it also ships the training code and the training datasets, including a 13 million sequence distillation set, so the model can be retrained from scratch. The published versions are research previews: the model is called OpenFold3-preview and the developers say the final model is still in development.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: header, Features, Datasets and Upcoming; technical report: Introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The model follows the AlphaFold 3 design and input features, which the developers set out to reproduce bitwise. Alignments are built either from the ColabFold server or with JackHMMER and hhblits following the AlphaFold 3 protocol, and templates can be supplied for protein monomers. Training follows the AlphaFold 3 supplementary information. For OpenFold3-preview2 that meant 155,000 steps in total, split into 131,500 steps of initial training, 8,000 steps of fine-tuning stage 1 and 15,500 steps of fine-tuning stage 2, on 256 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. Unlike AlphaFold 3 the team skipped the third fine-tuning stage and trained the PAE confidence head from the start. Inference can use kernel acceleration through cuEquivariance and DeepSpeed4Science, spread one job across several GPUs, and run in a low memory mode.
sections.source_locator: README: header, Features; technical report: Model Updates, Training

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three parameter sets are documented, each tied to a range of software releases. The current default is openbind-2025-06-30-174k, file of3-ob-2025-06-30-174k.pt, at 174,000 training steps, trained with what the README calls the forthcoming OpenFold3 architecture and a June 2025 training cutoff. The two earlier sets are marked deprecated: openfold3-p2-155k, file of3-p2-155k.pt, at 155,000 steps, and openfold3-p1, file of3_ft3_v1.pt, at 78,000 steps. Older parameters need an older release, for example pip install openfold3 < 0.5 for the preview2 weights, and setup_openfold must be rerun after changing version. A result must therefore name both the parameter set and the package version. The repository cites itself as version 0.4.2 with DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19001000, and the packaging file carries a fallback version of 0.5.1.

profile.summary: AttentiveFP (Attentive FP) is a graph neural network for molecular property prediction. It reads a molecule as a graph of atoms and bonds and learns a fixed-length vector for the whole molecule, a neural fingerprint, using a graph attention mechanism over node and edge features; that vector is then mapped to the property being predicted. It is a molecular architecture rather than a protein model, and it appears on this benchmark database because the DeepProtein benchmark trained it as a baseline on protein tasks.
profile.summary_source_locator: PubMed abstract 31408336; metadata.yml: description; DeepProtein full text, Structural-based learning

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A molecule is represented as a graph whose nodes are atoms and whose edges are bonds. Attention layers update the node and edge embeddings, and a readout step pools the node embeddings into one vector for the molecule, which a predictor head turns into the target property. The authors report that the learned features are interpretable and that feature visualisation suggests the model picks up nonlocal intramolecular interactions from the task it was trained on. In the DeepProtein benchmark the model is configured with three AttentiveFP layers, an AttentiveFP readout and node and edge embedding dimension 64.
sections.source_locator: PubMed abstract 31408336; DeepProtein full text, GNN variants

sections.title: Use as a benchmark baseline
sections.body: The DeepProtein benchmark trained AttentiveFP as one of its graph baselines. It does not call the authors' own code: its encoder wraps the AttentiveFPGNN and AttentiveFPReadout classes of the dgllife library, and the benchmark records DGLlife 0.3.2 in its software configuration. The benchmark also states that since its protein inputs are two dimensional, it adds edge information with edge featurisers for some graph networks. A result quoted against AttentiveFP on a protein task therefore describes a model the benchmark trained, not a checkpoint released by the AttentiveFP authors.
sections.source_locator: encoders.py: class DGL_AttentiveFP; DeepProtein full text, Software configuration and Figure 1 caption

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The official repository is a Code Ocean capsule export (licence dated 2019) with no version number and no trained weights: it ships the model code and Jupyter notebooks for drug discovery datasets. A result must therefore name the code commit and the training script used, not a checkpoint. This page read the repository at commit dda6708342ffe255ded73c459ad64214a4615542. For a protein result, name instead the benchmark library and encoder that produced it; the DeepProtein README states that its legacy graph encoders, DGL_AttentiveFP among them, are not available in its version 2 runtime.

profile.summary: Genie generates new protein backbones with a diffusion model. It represents a structure as a cloud of oriented residues: noise is added to and removed from the alpha carbon coordinates, while the network reasons over Frenet-Serret frames built from the backbone geometry, which give each residue a position and an orientation. Sampling runs the reverse diffusion for 1,000 steps and writes alpha carbon coordinates, with no sequence input. The published models were trained from scratch on filtered SCOPe domains or on AlphaFold predictions of SwissProt, and the authors report designability, diversity and novelty against RFdiffusion, FrameDiff and other generators. The model is small, 4.1 million parameters against RFdiffusion's 59.8 million.
profile.summary_source_locator: paper: title, Sections 2.2, 2.3, 3.2 and Datasets; README: header and Sampling

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The forward process adds Gaussian noise to the alpha carbon coordinates of a domain over a fixed variance schedule with 1,000 steps. The network is trained to predict the noise added at each step, following the usual denoising diffusion objective, so training reduces to fitting that noise prediction model. What makes the representation asymmetric is that the input is a point cloud while the reasoning is frame based: Frenet-Serret frames are constructed from the backbone geometry of the noised structure, giving each residue an orientation as well as a position, which the authors call equivariantly diffusing oriented residue clouds. The architecture uses pair transform layers, with triangular attention switched off in the shipped configuration. At sampling time the noise vector can be multiplied by a constant factor, in the manner of low temperature sampling, which trades designability against diversity.
sections.source_locator: paper: Sections 2.2, 2.3, Loss and 3.2; weights/scope_l_256/configuration

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The weights ship inside the repository rather than on a model hub. At the commit read here there are three sets, each with its own configuration file: weights/scope_l_128 with epoch=49999.ckpt, weights/scope_l_256 with epoch=29999.ckpt, and weights/swissprot_l_256 with epoch=99.ckpt. The names match the paper's variants: a model trained on SCOPe with a maximum length of 128, and the two long models, Genie-SCOPe and Genie-SwissProt, both with the maximum sequence length set to 256. The shipped configuration for scope_l_256 sets maximumNumResidues to 256, five pair transform layers, no triangular attention and a learning rate of 1e-4. A result should name the weight folder, the checkpoint epoch, the repository commit and the sampling noise scale, since that scale changes the output distribution.

limitations.text: Short proteins only. The released models cap at 128 or 256 residues, set in the configuration as maximumNumResidues.

Sampling is long: the reverse process runs 1,000 diffusion steps, and sampling time in the paper is reported as a function of those steps and the protein length.
The README's weight loading snippet names a file, weights/genie_l_128_epoch=49999.ckpt, that does not exist at the commit read; the checkpoints live in per-model subfolders instead.

profile.summary: AlphaFold-Multimer predicts the structure of a protein complex. It is the multi-chain mode of AlphaFold v2: the input is a FASTA file holding every chain of the complex, alignments are built against several sequence databases, and the system returns coordinates together with per-residue and per-pair confidence estimates, pTM and predicted aligned error. Five trained parameter sets are shipped, and by default each is run with five random seeds, giving 25 predictions that are ranked. It is the same code base as single chain AlphaFold, selected with one flag, and the developers call the multimer implementation a work in progress that is less stable than the monomer system.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: header, Model parameters and Running AlphaFold-Multimer; config.py: MODEL_PRESETS

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The pipeline has two halves. First a data pipeline searches genetic databases to build alignments and find templates: BFD, MGnify, PDB70, the PDB in mmCIF format, UniRef30, UniRef90, and for the multimer mode also PDB seqres and UniProt. Then the neural network predicts the structure, and the multimer models carry heads for a distogram, masked MSA, experimentally resolved atoms, predicted aligned error and predicted lDDT. The current weights come from the v2.3.0 update: the same architecture and training method as the AlphaFold-Multimer paper, fine tuned on PDB structures up to 2021-09-30 instead of 2018-04-30, with the training crop raised from 384 to 640 residues, the number of chains used at training raised from 8 to 20, and the maximum number of alignment sequences raised from 1,152 to 2,048 for three of the five models. The self-distillation set was also rebuilt from clustered MGnify with a looser cluster filter.
sections.source_locator: README: Genetic databases; technical note: whole document; config.py: heads

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The default multimer preset names five models, model_1_multimer_v3 through model_5_multimer_v3, and the parameter file for them is alphafold_params_2022-12-06.tar. Two older generations remain usable but deprecated: the v2.2.0 weights from alphafold_params_2022-03-02.tar, selected by changing _v3 to _v2 in the multimer presets, and the v2.1.0 weights from alphafold_params_2022-01-19.tar, selected by removing _v3. The code applies version-specific differences to the configuration, mostly for numerical stability. Reproducibility also depends on the database snapshot: the README warns that PDB seqres and the PDB mmCIF files must be from exactly the same date or template search for multimers can fail, and prediction uses a max_template_date cutoff given on the command line. A result should therefore name the parameter tar, the model preset, the number of seeds per model and the template date.
sections.source_locator: config.py: MODEL_PRESETS and the version difference comment; README: Model parameters, Using deprecated model weights, Updating existing installation and Running AlphaFold-Multimer

sections.title: When to prefer it
sections.body: The developers give a rule. The v2.3.0 multimer models are expected to be preferred whenever the stoichiometry of the complex is known, including for structures known to be monomeric. Where the stoichiometry is unknown, for instance in genome-scale prediction, single chain AlphaFold is likely to be more accurate on average, unless the chain runs to several thousand residues. For very large or difficult targets they suggest raising the number of seeds per model to 20, which is not the default because of the cost.

profile.summary: Graphormer is a transformer architecture for graphs, published by Microsoft Research for molecule modelling. It takes a graph, such as a molecule, and encodes the graph's structural information into a standard Transformer. The released package is a training toolkit for graph-level prediction tasks rather than one fixed model; it appears on this benchmark database because the DeepProtein benchmark trained a Graphormer layer as a baseline on protein tasks.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: opening paragraph; arXiv abstract; DeepProtein full text, GNN variants

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Graphormer keeps the standard transformer blocks and adds encodings that put the graph structure into the model: the paper describes structural encoding methods, which the benchmark paper summarises as spatial, centrality and edge encoding. The authors also give a mathematical characterisation of the expressive power of the architecture and argue that with these encodings many popular graph neural network variants are special cases of Graphormer. The package builds on a pinned fairseq revision, so training and inference run through the fairseq command line.
sections.source_locator: arXiv abstract; DeepProtein full text, Graphormer paragraph; README.md: Containerized legacy environment

sections.title: Use as a benchmark baseline
sections.body: The DeepProtein benchmark trained Graphormer as one of its graph baselines. It does not use the Microsoft package: its encoder imports GraphormerLayer from DGL, wraps it with a linear projection and max pooling, and the benchmark states that for simplicity and scalability on large graphs it deployed only one Graphormer layer with ReLU activation, node embedding dimension 64 and LayerNorm after the MLP layers. A protein result against the name Graphormer is therefore a single DGL Graphormer layer the benchmark trained, not a Microsoft Graphormer checkpoint.
sections.source_locator: DeepProtein full text, Graphormer paragraph; encoders.py: class Graphormer

sections.body: The repository is at version 2.0, released in December 2021, and its README states that pretrained models on PCQM4M and PCQM4Mv2 are available and that advanced pretrained versions are available only on Azure Quantum Elements. The README gives no download address for the pretrained models, so a result should name the code commit, the task script and the checkpoint path used. This page read the repository at commit c55f56923c2d7cd654161a6c84b28a2db65b5f3d. For a protein result, name the benchmark library instead; the DeepProtein README says its legacy graph encoders, Graphormer among them, are not available in its version 2 runtime.

strengths.text: The repository ships a container that pins the legacy fairseq, Python and CUDA stack the code needs, with a verification script, so the environment can be rebuilt years after release.
It supports the dataset interfaces of PyG, DGL, OGB and OCP, so existing graph datasets can be used without conversion code.

The authors report competition results for the architecture: first place in the quantum prediction track of the OGB Large-Scale Challenge (KDD Cup 2021) and a win in the Open Catalyst Challenge, both claims made by the developers in their README.

limitations.text: The code is on a legacy stack. The container pins Python 3.9, PyTorch 1.9.1 and CUDA 11.1 user space libraries, and the README states this is a reproducibility environment, not a claim of compatibility with current releases.

The better pretrained models are not open: the README says advanced pretrained versions are available exclusively on Azure Quantum Elements, and gives no download address for the PCQM4M models it does mention.
Multi-node training is out of scope for the supported setup, and the GPU path needs the NVIDIA Container Toolkit.
The benchmark result does not measure the published model. DeepProtein ran a single DGL Graphormer layer for scalability, and has since dropped that encoder from its version 2 runtime.

profile.summary: MPNN, the message passing neural network, is a general family of graph neural networks rather than a single trained model. A molecule or other graph is read as nodes and edges; the model learns a message passing algorithm and an aggregation procedure that compute a function of the whole graph, which is mapped to the property being predicted. The name appears on this benchmark database because the DeepProtein benchmark trained an MPNN as a baseline on protein tasks.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; DeepProtein full text, GNN variants

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: In the paper's framework, the model learns a message passing algorithm and an aggregation procedure that compute a function of the whole input graph. Unlike the simpler graph convolution and graph attention baselines, an MPNN uses edge features as well as node features. In the DeepProtein configuration the readout is Sum and Max and the node and edge embedding dimension is 64, with the number of message passing steps set by the encoder's num_timesteps argument.
sections.source_locator: arXiv abstract; DeepProtein full text, MPNN paragraph; encoders.py: class DGL_MPNN

sections.title: What has been released
sections.body: An open source implementation of the paper is at github.com/brain-research/mpnn under the Apache 2.0 licence. Its README states that it contains only the model class definition and some unit tests, that a dataset reader and basic trainer were planned for a future release, and that it is not an official Google product. It also notes that the default hyperparameters give reasonable performance on all targets but that the numbers in the paper came from a separate hyperparameter search with 50 trials per target. There are no trained weights.
sections.source_locator: README; LICENSE

sections.title: Use as a benchmark baseline
sections.body: The DeepProtein benchmark did not use the brain-research/mpnn reference code. Its encoder imports MPNNGNN from the dgllife library and adds a Sum and Max readout and a linear layer to the predictor dimension. A protein result reported against the name MPNN is therefore a dgllife message passing network that the benchmark trained on that task. The DeepProtein README states that its legacy graph encoders, DGL_MPNN among them, are not available in its version 2 runtime.

profile.summary: PAGTN, the path-augmented graph transformer network, is a graph neural network for molecular property prediction. Instead of only aggregating from immediate neighbours, it computes features of the paths between pairs of atoms and uses them to build global attention layers, so that distant parts of a molecule can influence each other directly. The authors trained it on quantum chemistry, physical chemistry and biochemistry property datasets; the name appears on this benchmark database because the DeepProtein benchmark trained it as a baseline on protein tasks.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; README.md: opening lines; DeepProtein full text, PAGTN paragraph

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The authors' starting point is that graph convolution networks rely on local aggregation and so can miss higher-order graph properties. The repository precomputes shortest paths in the molecular graph as a preprocessing step, and the paper uses path features in molecular graphs to build global attention layers. The repository's training script exposes the path length as a flag, with a maximum path length of 3 in the published command, along with position and ring embeddings, a hidden size of 160 and two attention heads. In the DeepProtein configuration the model is five PAGTN layers with LeakyReLU activation and node embedding dimension 64.
sections.source_locator: arXiv abstract; README.md: preprocessing and training commands; DeepProtein full text, PAGTN paragraph

sections.title: Use as a benchmark baseline
sections.body: The DeepProtein benchmark did not use the authors' repository. Its PAGTN encoder imports PAGTNGNN from the dgllife library and adds a weighted sum and max readout and a linear layer to the predictor dimension. The benchmark groups PAGTN with the graph transformers it added because, it says, graph transformers have recently shown their power in protein function prediction. A protein result against the name PAGTN is therefore a dgllife path-augmented network the benchmark trained, not a checkpoint from the authors.

sections.body: The repository has no releases, no version number and no trained weights: it ships the model code, the preprocessing script, the training script and the data and splits used in the paper as data.zip, plus the scripts that generated the published results. A result must therefore name the commit and the training flags used; this page read commit 4fd3606d49e81ebbe009aa9c69add16bd092d4d1. The README also gives two other model types behind the same script, a local variant selected with -mask_neigh and a convolutional network selected with -model_type conv_net, so a result must say which was run. For a protein result, name the benchmark library instead; the DeepProtein README says its legacy graph encoders, PAGTN among them, are not available in its version 2 runtime.

profile.summary: RoseTTAFold All-Atom predicts the structure of a biomolecular assembly from its parts. Inputs are given per chain: protein sequences as FASTA, nucleic acid strands as DNA or RNA FASTA, small molecules as SDF files, plus covalent bonds between a protein chain and a small molecule. The output is a PDB file with predicted lDDT in the B-factor column and a separate PyTorch file of confidence metrics, of which the developers' main one is pae_inter, the mean error of protein residues with respect to atom frames together with atom coordinates with respect to protein frames. They warn that the model is not accurate for all cases and say the error estimates are there to let users tell the good predictions from the bad, with pae_inter below 10 expected to mean a high quality dock.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: header, Inference Configs Using Hydra and Understanding model outputs

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Inference is driven by Hydra configuration files: a job inherits the base configuration and adds one entry per chain under protein_inputs, na_inputs, sm_inputs and covale_inputs. Alignments and templates are built by a script against UniRef30, BFD and a 2021 March snapshot of PDB100. The network settings in rf2aa/config/inference/base.yaml, the only model configuration in the sources read, sit under the key legacy_model_param and describe a RoseTTAFold style stack: 4 extra blocks, 32 main blocks and 4 refinement blocks, with MSA channels 256, full MSA channels 64, pair channels 192 and template channels 64, and SE(3) transformer layers of 32 channels and 2 degrees for structure refinement. It uses atom frames, chirality and Lennard-Jones terms. At inference the loader keeps up to 128 latent and 1,024 total alignment sequences and 4 templates, and recycles 4 times by default. The developers recommend keeping the defaults because they match the training task, but say raising MAXCYCLE to 10 gives better results on hard cases.
sections.source_locator: base.yaml: loader_params and legacy_model_param; README: Inference Configs Using Hydra and Setup

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One released checkpoint, RFAA_paper_weights.pt, downloaded from files.ipd.uw.edu and named as checkpoint_path in the default configuration. The sources read list no other weights, and the developers say they will share new models as they create them. Reproducibility also depends on the databases, which are pinned by name: UniRef30_2020_06, BFD, and PDB100 at 2021 March 03, plus legacy BLAST 2.2.26. A result should name the checkpoint, the repository commit, the MAXCYCLE setting and the database versions, and should state whether signalp6 was installed, since the Docker route leaves it out for licensing reasons and the predictions then do not use it.

profile.summary: GeoDock predicts the structure of a two-chain protein complex from the structures of the two partners. It takes the sequences and structures of the docking partners, with no multiple sequence alignment, and returns a docked complex in which the residues are allowed to move, so conformational change on binding can be predicted rather than assumed away. The network is a multitrack iterative transformer, and the point of it is speed: the authors report an average inference time of under one second on a single GPU, which makes large-scale screening possible. On the DIPS test set they report a 43 per cent top-1 success rate, falling to 31 per cent after removing close homologs they found contaminating the standard training split.
profile.summary_source_locator: paper: Abstract; README: header

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Conventional docking programs sample many candidate poses and rerank them, which is slow, and earlier deep learning dockers were faster but treated both partners as rigid bodies. GeoDock does neither. It is an iterative transformer over several tracks, taking the sequence and the structure of each partner, and it predicts the docked complex directly with residue-level flexibility. Because it takes structures rather than alignments, it fits the case where the individual structures are already known. The implementation depends on fair-esm, so language model embeddings of the sequences are part of the input pipeline. Inference is one call to a runner class with the two partner files.

A result should name the checkpoint and the package version, and should say whether the DIPS training split was decontaminated, because the paper reports success rates of 43 and 31 per cent for the same model on the contaminated and cleaned splits.

strengths.text: Fast enough for screening: the authors report under one second per complex on a single GPU, against the heavy sampling and reranking of conventional docking.
No alignment needed. Only the two partner structures and their sequences go in, which suits cases where the monomer structures are already known.
Residues are allowed to move, so binding-induced conformational change can in principle be predicted rather than assumed absent, as in rigid docking.
The authors found and reported contamination in the standard DIPS split themselves, and give the lower success rate after cleaning it, which is the figure to compare against.

The flexibility is a foundation rather than a finished capability: the authors say binding-induced conformational change remains a challenge because training and evaluation data are limited.
Two partners only. Everything in the sources read, from the runner arguments to the output chains A and B, is a pairwise dock.

GeoDock is a general two-chain docking model, not an affinity predictor: it returns a structure, and any affinity number in a benchmark comes from something built on top of it. profile.summary: Graphinity predicts the change in antibody-antigen binding affinity caused by a mutation, the quantity written as delta delta G. It takes the structures of the wild-type complex and of the mutant, builds an atomic graph around the mutated site in each, passes both through an equivariant graph neural network, subtracts the two embeddings and reads out one number. The authors report Pearson correlations up to 0.87 on 645 experimental single-point mutations, then show that this reflects overtraining on a few hundred data points rather than a generalisable model. To find out how much data would be needed they built synthetic sets of 942,723 FoldX and 20,829 Rosetta Flex ddG values, and conclude that orders of magnitude more experimental data are likely required, with diversity mattering as well as volume.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A structure goes in as a PDB file and becomes an atomic graph: non-hydrogen atoms are nodes, pairs of atoms less than 4 angstroms apart are edges, node features are a one-hot LibMolGrid atom type and edge features say whether the edge is within one binding partner or between the two. The graph is cut down to the neighbourhood of the mutated site: atoms on the mutated chain within 4 angstroms of the mutated residue, plus atoms on the partner chain within 4 angstroms of those. The network is three E(n) equivariant graph convolutional layers with a hidden dimension of 128. For a delta delta G prediction, the wild-type and mutant graphs are each passed through those layers and the embeddings subtracted, wild type minus mutant, before a final linear layer. Training used mean squared error, Adam at learning rate 0.001, batch size 32, dropout 0.2 on edges, weight decay 1e-16 and global max pooling as readout, for 500 epochs except on the large FoldX set where 10 epochs were used for cost.
sections.source_locator: paper: Methods, EGNN architecture

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There is no single released Graphinity model. The repository ships eight checkpoints from the data volume experiment, under example/ddg_synthetic/FoldX/varying_dataset_size/model_weights, each about 4.3 MB and named by the number of FoldX training examples it saw: subset_580, subset_900, subset_4500, subset_9000, subset_45000, subset_90000, subset_450000 and full_848597. They are illustrations of the data scaling question rather than a production predictor, so a result must name the checkpoint. The repository also keeps the experimental delta delta G datasets with their ten-fold cross-validation splits at CDR sequence identity cut-offs of 100, 90 and 70 per cent and a random split, under data/ddg_experimental. The environment is pinned hard, to Python 3.7.10, PyTorch 1.8.0 and PyTorch Geometric 1.6.3, with and without CUDA 10.2.

strengths.text: Small and quick to run: the bundled five-mutation test takes under 20 seconds, and the authors state Graphinity can be run without a GPU.

profile.summary: RFD4-Proteina designs proteins and biomolecular complexes, generating sequence and all-atom structure together rather than a backbone to be sequenced later. The design is specified either as an annotated CIF structure or as a short YAML condition spec, which can fix a motif, name hotspots, hold a binding target or a ligand, or constrain features such as burial and hydrogen bonds. One model covers monomers, protein and DNA binders, antibodies and nanobodies, enzyme motif scaffolding and small molecule pockets, and it can also refine an existing design by partial diffusion or search over generation paths scored by structure prediction oracles. It is a flow matching model in the latent space of a frozen autoencoder, so generation always loads two matched checkpoints. Code and weights are BSD 3-Clause, from the Baker Lab and NVIDIA GenAIR.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Two components are always loaded together. The autoencoder is frozen and unified: one encoder and decoder covering proteins, nucleic acids, DNA and modified residues, with 32 latent channels per residue and a residue vocabulary of 147 classes, trained to 400,000 steps. The denoiser is a flow matching latent model that generates in exactly that latent space, which is why the pair cannot be mixed across releases: the developers say mixing a flow model with a different autoencoder produces nonsense rather than an error. The released denoiser is a pretrained base at step 320,000 with a rank-32 LoRA fine-tune merged in, and by default it conditions the decoder on its own sequence readout during inference. Sampling runs 60 steps, with the trunk recycled a varying number of times per step: the three released presets, low, medium and high, come to 120, 180 and 300 trunk passes, medium being the default. Reward-guided search branches and prunes candidates at points in that schedule, scored by a refolding oracle such as OpenFold3.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The current release is the 2026-10-19 pair: rfd4-proteina-flow-release-2026-10-19 as the denoiser and rfd4-proteina-ae-release-2026-10-19 as the autoencoder, published under the stable names flow_checkpoints/rfd4_proteina_flow-ema.ckpt and ae_checkpoints/rfd4_proteina_ae-ema.ckpt, with SHA-256 sidecars and a release manifest. It supersedes the 2026-10-15 pair, which shared the architecture, and an earlier pair with a 16-dimensional latent and a 33-class vocabulary which is incompatible. The pretrained base and the LoRA adapter are published separately under base/ and adapter/, and the root bundle is exactly the two merged. The published checkpoints carry EMA weights and hyperparameters only, which is enough for inference or fine-tuning but not to resume a training run. Per release-checkpoints.json the released flow checkpoint is 1,751,488,703 bytes against 3,511,389,403 for its full training checkpoint, and the autoencoder 1,029,340,246 against 3,095,456,721. The model card states 1.74 GB and 4.21 GB for the flow pair, which does not match its own manifest: 4,211,265,195 bytes is the full size of a different file, flow_checkpoints/rfd4_proteina_flow_pretrain-ema.ckpt, and 1,742,660,596 is the size of model.safetensors. Reproducibility comes from pinning: configs/inference.yaml names the Hub repository and the revision, from_pretrained takes a revision argument, and the documentation tells users not to hard-code filenames anywhere else.

sections.title: What the developers claim, and how they qualify it
sections.body: The model card reports design efficiency as structurally distinct computational passers per GPU-hour, including generation and evaluation, on four internal benchmarks: 71.60 on 24 protein binder targets against 13.24 for the best comparator, 112.25 on 77 small-molecule binder targets against 15.48, 91.18 on 37 atomic motif enzyme targets against 26.02, and 41.97 on three DNA binder targets against 9.46. The developers attach three qualifications themselves. The numbers were measured on the previous release pair in a frozen benchmark of 9 October 2026 and have not been re-measured on the current checkpoints. The conditioning differs between methods in some comparisons, and only three DNA targets are included. And computational passers do not establish experimental activity.

profile.summary: IgLM is a generative language model for antibody sequences. Given an antibody heavy or light chain variable sequence with one span replaced by a mask, together with tags for the chain type and the species of origin, it generates replacement spans of variable length using the sequence on both sides of the mask, and it can also generate a whole chain from a short prompt or score an existing sequence. Its purpose is to build synthetic antibody libraries, for example diverse CDR loop libraries, from sequences that look like natural antibodies.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract and Methods: Infilling formulation; README: Command line usage

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: IgLM is a transformer decoder based on a modified GPT-2. A span of the antibody sequence is replaced by a single mask token, the remaining sequence is concatenated with a separator and then the span itself, and two conditioning tags for chain type and species are prepended, so an ordinary left-to-right language model learns to produce the missing span with the sequence on both sides available as context. In training the masked spans were ten to twenty residues long, chosen at random, so that spans of any position and length can be re-designed at inference. The released configuration is a 4-layer model with embedding size 512, 8 attention heads and a vocabulary of 33 tokens.
sections.source_locator: Paper Methods: Infilling formulation and Model implementation; config.json

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two sizes were trained: IgLM and IgLM-S, which the paper describes as 13M and 1.4M trainable parameters; its hyperparameter table gives total parameters of 12,889,600 and 1,439,616. Both checkpoints are bundled in the Python package, which selects them by name, and IgLM is the default. A result should name the checkpoint, the package version (setup.cfg declares 0.1.0) or the commit, and the sampling settings, because generation is stochastic and the paper varies temperature and nucleus probability.
sections.source_locator: Paper Results and Table 1; iglm/model/IgLM.py CHECKPOINT_DICT; setup.cfg

sections.title: Licence, and why it matters here
sections.body: The code and the pre-trained weights are released for non-commercial use under the JHU Academic Software License Agreement, which grants a non-exclusive, non-transferable licence to non-profit academic or research institutions only, and states that commercial use, including research use by for-profit entities, needs a separate written agreement. The README points commercial users at Johns Hopkins Technology Ventures. The licence also asks that publications using the software cite it.
sections.source_locator: README opening paragraph; LICENSE.md

sections.title: What the authors report
sections.body: The paper reports that infilled CDR loop libraries had better in silico developability profiles than the parent antibodies and that sequences infilled by IgLM were typically more human-like than their parents by OASis identity. The authors also note, citing other work, that antibody-specific language models have been found to underperform universal protein models on antibody fitness prediction tasks. These are the authors' claims, not measurements by Rewire.
sections.source_locator: Paper abstract, Results on human-likeness and Discussion

strengths.text: Spans are re-designed with the sequence on both sides as context, which is what distinguishes it from models that only decode from one end, and the span length is not fixed.
strengths.source_locator: Paper abstract and Methods: Infilling formulation

strengths.text: Generation is conditioned on chain type and species, so human heavy chains, camel nanobodies and other combinations can be requested with a token.
strengths.source_locator: README: Full antibody sequence generation; config.json conditioning flags

strengths.text: It is small and self-contained: the largest checkpoint has about 13M parameters, both checkpoints ship inside the pip package, and the dependencies are PyTorch and Transformers with no data download needed for inference.

The authors report that infilled libraries were more human-like than their parent antibodies by OASis identity and had better in silico developability profiles; these are their measurements, not ours.
strengths.source_locator: Paper abstract and Results on human-likeness

limitations.text: The licence is non-commercial: use is granted to non-profit academic and research institutions only, and research use by a for-profit entity needs a separate written agreement from Johns Hopkins.

It is an antibody-only model trained on the Observed Antibody Space: six species, heavily skewed towards human heavy chains, so other species and other protein families are out of its training distribution.
The context is 512 positions and the package generation call stops at 150 tokens, so it works on single variable domains rather than paired or full-length chains.

The authors note that antibody-specific language models have been found to underperform universal protein models on antibody fitness prediction, so this is a library design tool rather than a binding predictor.

run_guide.summary: Install the iglm package and re-design a CDR H3 span of an antibody, then score a sequence.
prerequisites: Acceptance of the JHU Academic Software License Agreement, which allows non-commercial use by non-profit academic or research institutions only.
Python with PyTorch 1.11 or above, Transformers 4.6.1 or above, tokenizers, biopython, numpy and tqdm, which setup.cfg declares as the dependencies.
A GPU is optional: the package selects a CUDA device when one is available and falls back to the CPU.
No data download is needed for inference: both checkpoints ship inside the package.

steps.title: Install
steps.shell: pip install iglm
steps.explanation: The install command the README gives.

steps.title: Re-design a CDR H3 span
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
from iglm import IgLM

iglm = IgLM()

parent_sequence = "EVQLVESGGGLVQPGGSLRLSCAASGFNIKEYYMHWVRQAPGKGLEWVGLIDPEQGNTIYDPKFQDRATISADNSKNTAYLQMNSLRAEDTAVYYCARDTAAYFDYWGQGTLVTVS"
chain_token = "[HEAVY]"
species_token = "[HUMAN]"
infill_range = (98, 106)
num_seqs = 100

generated_seqs = iglm.infill(
    parent_sequence,
    chain_token,
    species_token,
    infill_range=infill_range,
    num_to_generate=num_seqs,
)
print(generated_seqs[:3])
PY
steps.explanation: The README's package example for infilling, wrapped in a shell heredoc. It loads the default IgLM checkpoint and generates 100 unique variants of the 1JPT heavy chain with a re-designed span from position 98 to 106. A final print of the first three sequences was added by Rewire so the step shows its result.
steps.source_locator: README: Package usage, Re-design spans of an antibody sequence

steps.title: Score a sequence
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
import math
from iglm import IgLM

iglm = IgLM()

sequence = "EVQLVESGGGLVQPGGSLRLSCAASGFNIKEYYMHWVRQAPGKGLEWVGLIDPEQGNTIYDPKFQDRATISADNSKNTAYLQMNSLRAEDTAVYYCARDTAAYFDYWGQGTLVTVS"
chain_token = "[HEAVY]"
species_token = "[HUMAN]"

log_likelihood = iglm.log_likelihood(
    sequence,
    chain_token,
    species_token,
)
perplexity = math.exp(-log_likelihood)
print(log_likelihood, perplexity)
PY
steps.explanation: The README's package example for sequence evaluation, wrapped in a shell heredoc, with a print of the two values added by Rewire. It returns the log likelihood of the sequence under the given chain and species conditioning and the corresponding perplexity.

outputs: A list of unique infilled antibody sequences, 100 in the example, as the README describes the infill call.
A log likelihood and a perplexity for the scored sequence.

The command line entry points iglm_infill, iglm_generate and iglm_evaluate exist as console scripts, but the README examples for them use a fasta file under data/antibodies/ that is not in the repository tree read here.
Generation is stochastic: the number of sequences, the temperature and the nucleus probability change the result, so a run should record them.

profile.summary: Bacformer is a model of whole bacterial genomes. It takes the proteins of a genome, ordered by their coordinates on the chromosome and plasmids, embeds each one with a protein language model, and runs a transformer over those per-protein vectors so that every protein is represented in the context of the rest of the genome. The base size uses ESM-2 t12 35M embeddings in a 12-layer transformer of hidden size 480, was pretrained on about 1.3 million bacterial genomes and about 3 billion proteins, and is used for tasks such as strain clustering, operon identification, essential gene prediction and protein-protein interaction prediction.
profile.summary_source_locator: README opening paragraph and Requirements; model card opening and Architecture

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Every protein of a genome is embedded with a base protein language model and the amino acid token embeddings are averaged into one vector, so one protein is one token. Those tokens are fed in genomic order into a transformer of 12 layers and hidden size 480 for the base size, with rotary positional embeddings for order and learnable contig embeddings that mark which chromosome or plasmid a protein came from. Pretraining predicts the protein family of a masked or next protein out of 50 thousand clusters, while the input remains the exact protein sequence, so single-residue differences stay visible.
sections.source_locator: README opening paragraph; model card: Architecture

sections.title: Checkpoints in this family
sections.body: The README table lists eight checkpoints. It describes bacformer-masked-MAG and bacformer-causal-MAG as 26M parameter models pretrained on about 1.3 million metagenome-assembled genomes, with a masked and an autoregressive objective; bacformer-masked-complete-genomes and bacformer-causal-complete-genomes as those two MAG models finetuned on about 40 thousand complete genomes; bacformer-large-masked-MAG and bacformer-large-masked-complete-genomes with the same text, a 300M parameter model pretrained on the MAG corpus with a masked objective; bacformer-causal-protein-family-modeling-complete-genomes as bacformer-causal-MAG finetuned on about 40 thousand complete genomes with protein-family tokens as input; and bacformer-for-essential-genes-prediction as bacformer-masked-complete-genomes finetuned on the essential-genes prediction task. The preprint gives the complete-genome set as 48,932 genomes. Bacformer Large has its own record.
sections.source_locator: README: Pretrained model checkpoints table

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: A result must name the checkpoint and the Hugging Face revision, because the eight checkpoints differ in objective, corpus and size. The two base MAG checkpoints were served at revisions 340a08cf5d5cd7d9f1ffac9075cde733d108a82b (masked) and e4c8d6dc4decaa88729ce3853b1f329fee3b4960 (causal) on 2026-11-27, both created on 2025-03-19 and both reporting 50,852,241 parameters. The README also records that a bug in the Bacformer Large code on Hugging Face was fixed on 2025-05-15, which matters for the large size.

sections.title: What it is used for
sections.body: The README names strain clustering, essential gene prediction, operon identification, protein-protein interaction prediction and protein function prediction, and ships tutorials for several of them. The preprint reports that the authors used the model to predict protein-protein interactions, uncover operon structure, infer phenotypic traits including antimicrobial resistance, and design template synthetic proteomes.

strengths.text: The genome, not the single protein, is the unit of modelling: each protein embedding depends on the other proteins present, which is what the authors report lets the model recover interactions and operon structure.

One pretrained model serves several bacterial genomics tasks: the README names strain clustering, essential gene prediction, operon identification, protein-protein interaction prediction and protein function prediction, with tutorials for several of them.
Code and the checkpoints read here are Apache-2.0 and the Hugging Face repositories are not gated, so the family can be used without an access request.
strengths.source_locator: Repository LICENSE; model card front matter; Hugging Face API gated field

strengths.text: Both a masked and an autoregressive variant are released at each stage, so the same architecture can be used for representation tasks and for generation of protein-family sequences.

limitations.text: A base protein language model is part of the pipeline: ESM-2 t12 35M for Bacformer and ESM-C for Bacformer Large, which must embed every protein before Bacformer runs.
Genomes are limited to 6,000 proteins in pretraining, so larger protein sets must be cut or split.

The install route expects PyTorch 2.2 or above with flash attention and the usage examples select a CUDA device, so a GPU machine is assumed; the README adds a troubleshooting path with a CUDA 12.1 conda environment.

No model card or Hugging Face metadata is saved here for two of the eight listed checkpoints, the protein-family generation model and the essential-genes finetune, so this record describes them only from the README table.

run_guide.summary: Install the bacformer package and compute contextual protein embeddings for a few protein sequences with a base-size Bacformer checkpoint.
prerequisites: Python 3.10, which the README names as the version Bacformer was developed in.
PyTorch 2.2 or above and flash attention, as the README install section asks for.
A CUDA GPU: the README usage examples set device to cuda:0.
Network access to Hugging Face for the Bacformer checkpoint and the ESM-2 t12 35M base model.

steps.title: Install
steps.shell:
pip install "torch>=2.2"
pip install flash-attn --no-build-isolation
pip install bacformer
steps.explanation: The three install commands the README gives, in the order it gives them.

steps.title: Embed a few protein sequences
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForMaskedLM
from bacformer.pp import protein_seqs_to_bacformer_inputs

device = "cuda:0"
masked_model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained("macwiatrak/bacformer-masked-MAG", trust_remote_code=True).to(torch.bfloat16).eval().to(device)

protein_sequences = [
    "MGYDLVAGFQKNVRTI",
    "MKAILVVLLG",
    "MQLIESRFYKDPWGNVHATC",
    "MSTNPKPQRFAWL",
]
inputs = protein_seqs_to_bacformer_inputs(
    protein_sequences,
    device=device,
    batch_size=128,

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each protein sequence of a genome is first embedded with a base protein language model and the amino acid token embeddings are averaged into one vector per protein. Those vectors are the tokens of a transformer of 12 layers and hidden size 480, which attends over all proteins of the genome and so returns contextual protein embeddings.     device=device,

    max_n_proteins=6000,
)

print(outputs.keys())

profile.summary: Bacformer Large is the larger of the two Bacformer sizes. Like the base size it treats a whole bacterial genome as a sequence of proteins ordered along the chromosome and plasmids, but it embeds each protein with ESM-C 300M and runs a 30-layer transformer of hidden size 960 over those per-protein vectors, returning an embedding for each protein that depends on the rest of the genome. Two checkpoints are released: bacformer-large-masked-MAG, pretrained on about 1.3 million metagenome-assembled genomes, and bacformer-large-masked-complete-genomes, which is listed for complete genomes and whose Hugging Face metadata gives bacformer-large-masked-MAG as its base model.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card opening, What is new and Architecture; README: News and Requirements; Hugging Face API cardData.base_model for the complete-genomes checkpoint

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each protein of a genome is embedded with ESM-C 300M and the amino acid token embeddings are averaged into one 960-dimensional vector, so one protein is one token. The tokens are fed in genomic order into a 30-layer transformer of hidden size 960 that uses SwiGLU activations, rotary positional embeddings for order and learnable contig embeddings for chromosome and plasmid structure. Pretraining predicts the protein family of masked proteins out of 50 thousand clusters, while the input stays the exact protein sequence.
sections.source_locator: Model card: What is new in Bacformer Large, Architecture and Transformer backbone

sections.title: What distinguishes this size
sections.body: The card lists the differences from the base size: more than 300M parameters, SwiGLU activations, ESM-C 300M instead of ESM-2 as the base protein language model, no special tokens, and the forward argument renamed from token_type_ids to contig_ids. The Hugging Face safetensors index reports 431,765,841 parameters for both large checkpoints. The README says the release of Bacformer Large brought improved performance on downstream tasks.

A result must name the checkpoint and the revision, and in particular must be later than the fix the README records on 2025-05-15 for a bug in the Bacformer Large code on Hugging Face that lowered embedding quality.

steps.title: Embed a few protein sequences with Bacformer Large
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoModel
from bacformer.pp import protein_seqs_to_bacformer_inputs

device = "cuda:0"
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(
    "macwiatrak/bacformer-large-masked-MAG", trust_remote_code=True
).to(device).eval().to(torch.bfloat16)

protein_sequences = [
    "MGYDLVAGFQKNVRTI",
    "MKAILVVLLG",
    "MQLIESRFYKDPWGNVHATC",
    "MSTNPKPQRFAWL",
]
inputs = protein_seqs_to_bacformer_inputs(
    protein_sequences,
    device=device,
    batch_size=128,
    max_n_proteins=6000,
    bacformer_model_type="large",
)

with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model(**inputs, return_dict=True)
print('last hidden state shape:', outputs["last_hidden_state"].shape)
PY

profile.summary: bacformer-large-masked-complete-genomes is one released checkpoint of Bacformer, a model that treats a whole bacterial genome as a sequence of proteins ordered along the chromosome and plasmids. Each protein is embedded with the base protein language model ESM-C 300M and the averaged embedding is used as one token, so the transformer returns, for every protein, a representation that depends on the other proteins in the same genome. This checkpoint was trained with a masked objective, predicting the protein family of masked proteins, on the MAG corpus of about 1.3 million metagenome-assembled genomes and then about 40 thousand complete genomes from NCBI RefSeq.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: opening section and Training Data; README opening paragraph

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each protein sequence of a genome is first embedded with a base protein language model and the amino acid token embeddings are averaged into one vector per protein. Those vectors are the tokens of a transformer of 30 layers and hidden size 960, which attends over all proteins of the genome and so returns contextual protein embeddings. Position is encoded with rotary positional embeddings and learnable contig embeddings mark which chromosome or plasmid each protein came from. The pretraining head does not predict amino acids: it predicts a discrete protein family index out of 50 thousand clusters, while the input stays the exact protein sequence.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Architecture, Input embeddings and Transformer backbone

sections.title: What distinguishes this checkpoint
sections.body: The model card describes this checkpoint as a 300M-parameter transformer further pretrained on about 40 thousand complete genomes from NCBI RefSeq, starting from the matching metagenome-assembled-genome checkpoint. Its objective is masked: 15 per cent of the proteins are masked and their protein families are predicted from the rest of the genome. It takes protein embeddings from ESM-C 300M.
sections.source_locator: Model card: opening section, Training Data and Training objective

sections.body: A result should name the Hugging Face repository macwiatrak/bacformer-large-masked-complete-genomes and the revision it used; this page was written from revision 84f85c37a05e55559142b842c1569e265183b554, which the Hugging Face API reported on 2026-11-27. The README table lists eight checkpoints. It describes bacformer-masked-MAG and bacformer-causal-MAG as 26M parameter models pretrained on about 1.3 million metagenome-assembled genomes, with a masked and an autoregressive objective; bacformer-masked-complete-genomes and bacformer-causal-complete-genomes as those two MAG models finetuned on about 40 thousand complete genomes; bacformer-large-masked-MAG and bacformer-large-masked-complete-genomes with the same text, a 300M parameter model pretrained on the MAG corpus with a masked objective; bacformer-causal-protein-family-modeling-complete-genomes as bacformer-causal-MAG finetuned on about 40 thousand complete genomes with protein-family tokens as input; and bacformer-for-essential-genes-prediction as bacformer-masked-complete-genomes finetuned on the essential-genes prediction task. The README row for this checkpoint repeats the MAG wording, while its model card describes further pretraining on about 40 thousand complete genomes. The README also records that a bug in the Bacformer Large code on Hugging Face was fixed on 2025-05-15 and that models downloaded or cached before that date should be downloaded again, which matters for this checkpoint.

steps.title: Load the checkpoint and embed a few proteins
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
from bacformer.pp import embed_dataset_col
from datasets import load_dataset


# load the operon dataset from long-read RNA sequencing
operon_dataset = load_dataset("macwiatrak/operon-identification-long-read-rna-sequencing", split="test")

# embed the protein sequences with Bacformer
# we compute contextualised protein embeddings for all proteins in the genome
operon_dataset = embed_dataset_col(
    dataset=operon_dataset,
    model_path="macwiatrak/bacformer-masked-complete-genomes",
    max_n_proteins=9000,
    genome_pooling_method=None,  # set to None to get embeddings for all proteins in the genome
    model_type="bacformer",  # for Bacformer 26M model, use "bacformer_large" for Bacformer Large 300M
)
PY

steps.title: Load the checkpoint and embed a few proteins
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForMaskedLM
from bacformer.pp import protein_seqs_to_bacformer_inputs

device = "cuda:0"
masked_model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained("macwiatrak/bacformer-masked-MAG", trust_remote_code=True).to(torch.bfloat16).eval().to(device)

protein_sequences = [
    "MGYDLVAGFQKNVRTI",
    "MKAILVVLLG",
    "MQLIESRFYKDPWGNVHATC",
    "MSTNPKPQRFAWL",
]
inputs = protein_seqs_to_bacformer_inputs(
    protein_sequences,
    device=device,
    batch_size=128,
    max_n_proteins=6000,
)

with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = masked_model(**inputs, return_dict=True)
print(outputs.keys())
PY

profile.summary: BioEmu-2 is a generative model from Microsoft Research that produces three dimensional all-atom structures for a biomolecular system given its chemical composition. Rather than returning a single predicted structure, it samples an ensemble of plausible structures by reverse diffusion, so a user can look at how a system moves between states; it can also propagate a set of sampled structures forward in time. The input is one or more biomolecular sequences, optionally with a multiple sequence alignment, contact conditioning and method conditioning, and systems may contain proteins, nucleic acids, ligands and other chemical components.
profile.summary_source_locator: MODEL_CARD.md: opening paragraph and Model summary table; README.md: Key features

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The model card describes BioEmu-2 as a diffusion-based all-atom score model with approximately 500M parameters. Structures are generated by reverse diffusion from noise, conditioned on the chemical composition of the system and optionally on an alignment, on contacts between specific atoms and on a method label. Because sampling is generative, the same input can be sampled many times to give an ensemble rather than one answer, and the authors say structure prediction can be guided by user-supplied information about distances between specific atoms. The code also offers steering samplers that favour structures with chosen properties, and an implicit transfer operator mode that generates a structure a chosen lag time later.
sections.source_locator: MODEL_CARD.md: Model summary and Key model capabilities; README.md: Key features and Steer sampling

sections.title: What it was trained on
sections.body: The model card lists the training sets with the number of training sequences or systems in each. Experimental structures come from the PDB in the Boltz-1 preprocessing (189,745 systems). Seven sets of molecular dynamics trajectories generated inside Microsoft contribute between 170 and 7,164 systems each. The largest contributions are AI-predicted structures: 7,231,107 AFDB monomers, 753,271 AFDB homodimer multiconformation systems, 22,157 AFDB heterodimer systems and 50,651 Teddymer systems. The card states that training used only publicly available data and data generated in-house by Microsoft, and that the training dates were August to September 2026.
sections.source_locator: MODEL_CARD.md: Training data table and paragraph, Model summary table

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One checkpoint is published, named bioemu2-preview, which load_model downloads by default from the microsoft/bioemu2 repository on Hugging Face. The model card gives no version number for the model itself, states a release date of October 2026 and says the same checkpoint was used for every benchmark it reports. A result should therefore name the code commit, the checkpoint name and the Hugging Face revision; this page read code at commit 8d4a2b7238716a94543ceaf411dfe32f99c1ae7c and the Hugging Face repository at revision dd4b0c1b69984b68edcb6200a544213be4d75242. Sampling is stochastic, so a reproducible run must also fix the sampler and the number of samples; the checkpoint documentation shows the precision defaults, which can be changed to full precision.

profile.summary: The All-Atom Structure Tokenizer turns a three dimensional biomolecular structure into a short list of integers and back again. Its encoder reads an assembly of heavy atoms, with its chemical graph, and emits one integer per chemical unit (a protein residue, a nucleotide, or a single ligand atom or ion) from a vocabulary of 8,192 identifiers. A separate coordinate decoder takes those integers, the chemical inventory of the assembly and Gaussian noise and reconstructs atomic coordinates. It is published as a PyTorch reference implementation of the tokenizer described in a Scinetics technical report on AtomLM-9b; the authors' trained checkpoints are not distributed, so the released code starts from random parameters.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: opening paragraphs and Architecture table

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The atom graph joins all covalent bonds plus up to 32 intramolecular and 16 intermolecular spatial neighbours per receiver within 12 angstroms. An atom encoder of 8 scalar and vector blocks (256 scalar and 64 vector channels) feeds a unit encoder that pools inside each unit and then runs 4 full-assembly attention layers at width 512. An invariant readout projects scalars, vector norms, inner products and ordered signed volumes from 512 down to 5 values, and finite scalar quantisation with levels (8, 8, 8, 4, 4) maps those to mixed-radix identifiers 0 to 8191, trained with a straight-through estimator. The coordinate decoder is 12 unit transformer layers at width 768 plus 4 equivariant atom blocks at scalar width 256, and samples coordinates from centred Gaussian noise with 50 Heun steps by default. Decoding an identifier recovers the five discrete levels exactly, but the step from levels to coordinates is learned and stochastic.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Architecture table and the paragraph below it

sections.title: What the input must look like
sections.body: An assembly is a JSON record with three ordered arrays: units, each with a kind (protein, dna, rna, ligand, ion or modified), a component name, chain, molecule and chain-relative position; atoms, each with a unit index, element and atom-role name, and optional charge, aromatic flag and xyz coordinates in angstroms; and bonds, listed once each as a pair of atom indices with a bond order, where 4 means aromatic. The card is explicit that standardisation is the user's job: biological assembly expansion from PDB or mmCIF, ligand bond perception and chemical component dictionary standardisation are upstream preprocessing steps. Atom and unit ordering must be preserved between encoding and decoding, and the command line tool stores a fingerprint of the chemical records with the identifiers and checks it before decoding. A unit with no observed atoms gets the sentinel -1 from the encoder and needs a valid identifier supplied before sampling.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Molecular inputs; examples/peptide_ligand.json

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The package is version 0.1.0 and requires Python 3.10 or later with torch 2.4 or later; its only console script is atomtoken. This page read Hugging Face revision 4c231da23f4d3be880d9e0b9ab8a62e49d8477bd. No trained checkpoint is published, and the card warns that identifiers produced by different checkpoints need not have the same structural meaning, so a token list is only comparable within one checkpoint. The card also states that the repository does not reproduce the report's benchmark scores. Two training profiles are selectable, tiny and report, the latter being the default; a result must therefore name the profile, the checkpoint file and the decoder seed, since decoding is stochastic and deterministic only with a fixed noise seed.

strengths.text: The input schema is defined precisely, down to bond orders, formal charges, missing coordinates and the handling of inter-chain links, and a worked example file ships with the code.
It is not protein-only: units may be protein residues, DNA, RNA, ligand atoms, ions or modified components, so a mixed assembly can be tokenised in one pass.

The released tests cover the discrete bottleneck in detail, including all 8,192 identifiers, rotation and translation behaviour, chirality signs, missing coordinates and deterministic decoding with a fixed seed.
A short end-to-end example runs on the shipped data: train for two steps on the tiny profile, then encode and decode with that checkpoint.

limitations.text: There are no trained weights. Anything useful requires training the tokenizer yourself, and the card says the release does not reproduce the report's benchmark scores.

Token identifiers are not a shared vocabulary: the card states that identifiers from different checkpoints need not have the same structural meaning, so tokens cannot be compared across training runs.
No licence is stated anywhere in the sources read, so the terms for reusing the code are unclear.

limitations.text: Preparing the input is the user's work: the model needs a standardised heavy-atom record with an explicit chemical graph, and assembly expansion, bond perception and component standardisation are left to upstream tools.
