profile.summary: MochiBind predicts which of two antibodies binds a given antigen more strongly, from sequence alone. Antibody and antigen sequences are embedded with a pretrained protein language model, mean-pooled to one vector each, concatenated, projected into a shared latent space and scored by a small multilayer perceptron that outputs the relative binding strength of the pair. Pairwise scores for a large antibody pool are then turned into a global ranking, so the model is aimed at screening candidate antibodies rather than giving an absolute affinity. Because no structure is needed, it can be run over pools of thousands of antibodies on CPU.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Summary, Results introduction and STAR Methods, Method details

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each residue of the antibody and antigen sequences is embedded by ESM-2 (esm2_t36_3B_UR50D) with embedding dimension 2560. Mean pooling over residues gives one fixed-length vector per sequence; the antigen and antibody vectors are concatenated into a 5120-dimensional representation. A learnable projection layer of dimension 1024 maps that into a shared latent space, and a multilayer perceptron head with layers [256, 128, 64] predicts the relative binding strength between the two antibodies of a pair. Training minimises a mean squared error loss, so the model is pushed to get both the sign and the size of the affinity difference right, with learning rate 0.001, batch size 32, dropout 0.3, the Adam optimiser and early stopping after five epochs without an improvement in holdout loss. Pairwise predictions are turned into a global ranking with the TrueSkill algorithm.
sections.source_locator: Paper: STAR Methods, Method details and Key resources table

sections.title: What it was trained on
sections.body: Training and evaluation use the AlphaBind dataset, which holds four antigen systems, each with thousands of experimentally characterised antibody candidates over a wide affinity range: AAB-PP489 (a single-chain variable fragment against human TIGIT), Pembrolizumab-scFv against PD-1, VHH72 (a camelid single-chain antibody against the SARS-CoV-1 receptor binding domain) and Trastuzumab-scFv against human HER2. The paper states that each antigen system contains approximately 30 000 antibody variants generated and validated with AlphaSeq. The released repository ships pretrained checkpoints for the four antigen systems, which the README lists as PEM, PP489, TRA and VHH72, together with sampled training, validation and test files from that data.
sections.source_locator: Paper: STAR Methods, Data source and preprocessing; README.md: checkpoint and data directories

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There is one release, the code deposited with the paper, and four checkpoints, one per antigen system. The repository is deliberately frozen: it states that the code is released solely for academic and scientific reproducibility and that pull requests are not accepted so the code stays exactly as it was used in the paper. A result should therefore name the commit and which checkpoint was used; this page read commit 0c693d815f7f0bf0a3dd5494205dca10fbc20c04. Full training is not reproducible from the repository alone: it expects precomputed ESM mean embedding files under a data_processed_esm_mean directory, which the user generates first.

profile.summary: ESMC (ESM Cambrian) is a family of protein language models that read an amino acid sequence and return per-residue representations and masked-residue predictions. The models are trained on billions of protein sequences, so the representations can be used as features or fine-tuned for downstream tasks such as variant effect prediction or protein engineering. Three sizes are published, with approximately 300M, 600M and 6B parameters; the 6B model also serves as the frozen backbone of the ESMFold2 structure predictor and of a set of sparse autoencoders released for interpretation.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: Model Details and Parameters; README.md: ESMC section

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ESMC is a transformer trained with masked language modelling over protein sequences. The model card states it uses pre-layer normalisation, rotary position embeddings and SwiGLU activations, with no biases in the linear layers or layer norms. The 6B model has 80 layers; the card's parameter table gives 30 layers for the 300M variant and 36 for the 600M. Training ran in two stages: one million steps at a context length of 512 with metagenomic data at 64 per cent of the mixture, then 500,000 steps at a context length of 2048 with metagenomic data reduced to 37.5 per cent. Beyond the final layer, hidden states from all layers can be returned, and pretrained sparse autoencoders decompose the 6B model's hidden states into interpretable features.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Model Architecture, Parameters, Training Procedure and Usage; README.md: ESMC Sparse Autoencoders

sections.title: Sizes and what they were trained on
sections.body: The card's table gives three scales: ESMC-300M with 30 layers and 1.26e22 training FLOPs, ESMC-600M with 36 layers and 2.17e22, and ESMC-6B with 80 layers and 2.37e23. The Hugging Face metadata gives exact counts from the stored tensors: 332,997,184 parameters for ESMC-300M, 575,036,992 for ESMC-600M and 6,352,005,184 for ESMC-6B. Training sequences come from UniRef, MGnify and the Joint Genome Institute, clustered at 70 per cent sequence identity into 83M, 372M and 2B clusters respectively. All three variants are described as publicly released, and none of the three repositories is gated.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Parameters, Model Variants and Training Data; Hugging Face API responses

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two generations of weights exist under the same name. The December 2024 weights, esmc-300m-2024-12 and esmc-600m-2024-12, were released in the esm package format; their card now says they are kept for backwards compatibility and recommends the Hugging Face compatible weights at biohub/ESMC-6B, biohub/ESMC-600M or biohub/ESMC-300M instead. Benchmark results that name ESM-C 300M or ESM-C 600M were produced with the older repositories. The developer organisation has also been renamed: requests for EvolutionaryScale repositories now resolve to biohub ones. A result should therefore name the repository, the revision and which generation of weights was used; this page read biohub/ESMC-600M at revision 5e366569e675ad5ae3512f66bf0b53ffe80ee83e and the legacy card at revision 7f10b20ae75017b2dbc884070e03434515709a8d.

run_guide.summary: Install the esm package and run ESMC-600M on one sequence through the Transformers API to get its logits.
prerequisites: Python with PyTorch; the card lists GPU compute requirements and recommends a GPU-enabled PyTorch environment.
Hugging Face Transformers v5.16.0 or later for the ESMC support, which pip install esm brings in.

steps.title: Run ESMC on one sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForMaskedLM, AutoTokenizer

GFP = "MSKGEELFTGVVPILVELDGDVNGHKFSVSGEGEGDATYGKLTLKFICTTGKLPVPWPTLVTTFSYGVQCFSRYPDHMKQHDFFKSAMPEGYVQERTIFFKDDGNYKTRAEVKFEGDTLVNRIELKGIDFKEDGNILGHKLEYNYNSHNVYIMADKQKNGIKVNFKIRHNIEDGSVQLADHYQQNTPIGDGPVLLPDNHYLSTQSALSKDPNEKRDHMVLLEFVTAAGITHGMDELYK"

model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained("biohub/ESMC-600M", device_map="auto").eval()
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("biohub/ESMC-600M")

inputs = tokenizer(GFP, return_tensors="pt", padding=True)
inputs = {k: v.to(model.device) for k, v in inputs.items()}

with torch.inference_mode():
    output = model(**inputs)

print(f"logits shape: {tuple(output.logits.shape)}")
PY
steps.explanation: The model card's example, wrapped in a shell heredoc. The card's own code loads biohub/ESMC-6B and says in a comment that biohub/ESMC-600M or biohub/ESMC-300M may be used instead; the smaller repository is chosen here. The sequence is the card's example GFP sequence.

steps.title: Return all layers instead of the last
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
# after building `inputs` and `model` as above
output = model(**inputs, output_hidden_states=True)
PY
steps.explanation: The card's one-line change for getting hidden states from every transformer layer rather than the final layer only; useful when the embeddings are to be used as features.

outputs: The printed shape of the per-residue logits tensor for the example sequence.
With output_hidden_states set, a tuple of hidden states, one per transformer layer.
A cached copy of the chosen ESMC repository in the local Hugging Face cache.

The Python example is the card's code placed in a shell heredoc, and the repository name was changed from ESMC-6B to ESMC-600M, which the card's own comment offers as an option.

profile.summary: AbMPNN designs antibody sequences for a given antibody structure. It is ProteinMPNN, an inverse folding model that proposes an amino acid sequence for a supplied backbone, fine-tuned by its authors on antibody data so that it does better on antibodies, in particular on the hypervariable CDR-H3 loop. The input is a backbone structure, optionally the antibody in complex with its antigen, and the output is one or more sequences for the positions being designed. The authors published the fine-tuned weights as a Zenodo deposit; there is no separate AbMPNN codebase, since the weights load into the ProteinMPNN code.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract and section 1; arXiv abstract page; Zenodo record description

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Inverse folding asks, given a backbone structure, which sequences would fold into that shape. ProteinMPNN factorises the sequence probability autoregressively: at each step it predicts one residue given the structure and the residues already decoded, with the order chosen at random rather than left to right, so context on both sides is available. The encoder takes distances between the N, CA, C, O and virtual CB atoms of the 48 nearest residues in space, decomposed into Gaussian radial basis functions, plus a relative positional encoding of the separation in the sequence and a token marking whether two residues are in different chains; node features start as a zero vector and are updated by a three-layer message passing network, with the edge features also updated. AbMPNN keeps this architecture and changes only the weights, by fine-tuning on antibody data.
sections.source_locator: Paper: section 2, Inverse folding with ProteinMPNN

sections.title: How it was fine-tuned
sections.body: Training starts from the published ProteinMPNN weights and proceeds in two stages: first on antibody structures predicted by ABodyBuilder2 from paired sequences in the Observed Antibody Space, then on antigen-binding fragments in complex from the Structural Antibody Database. Both stages use Adam, starting at a learning rate of 5 times 10 to the minus 4 for the OAS stage and 10 to the minus 4 for the SAbDab stage, with the rate cut tenfold when the validation loss has not improved for 10 epochs, or 5 epochs in the OAS stage. Each epoch consists of 1000 randomly selected antigen binding fragments. Clustering gives 107961 clusters for OAS and 1701 for the SAbDab complexes, and the authors place any SAbDab sequence that would have clustered with an OAS training or validation cluster into the SAbDab training set to avoid leakage. The OAS structures are modelled and hold no antigen, so epitope context is present only in the SAbDab stage.
sections.source_locator: Paper: section 3, data and training

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One set of weights is published: the Zenodo deposit 10.5281/zenodo.8164693, dated 19 July 2023, holding abmpnn.pt together with oas_splits.csv and sabdab_splits.csv, under CC BY 4.0. The deposit is a dataset record with no version string, and its description says the model is based on ProteinMPNN and can be run with that code. There is no AbMPNN repository, so a result should name the Zenodo DOI for the weights and the ProteinMPNN commit used to run them; this page read ProteinMPNN at commit 8907e6671bfbfc92303b5f79c4b5e6ce47cdef57. Sampling is stochastic, so the sampling temperature and seed also belong in any report; the paper used a sampling temperature of 0.2 for its SAbDab test set.
sections.source_locator: Zenodo record metadata and description; Paper: section 4; ProteinMPNN README.md: input flags

strengths.text: The weights are published openly under CC BY 4.0, and they drop into the existing ProteinMPNN code, so no new software is needed.
strengths.source_locator: Zenodo record metadata and description; ProteinMPNN README.md

strengths.text: The authors report the largest gains on CDR-H3, the loop they describe as the most diverse and usually the most important for antigen recognition; that is their claim about their own model.
The dataset splits used for fine-tuning are published with the weights, so a comparison can respect the same train, validation and test division.
strengths.source_locator: Zenodo record metadata: files and description

strengths.text: Order-agnostic decoding suits antibodies: the framework regions can be held fixed while the CDR loops are designed with context on both sides.

limitations.text: It designs sequences for a structure you already have: a backbone must be supplied, from experiment or from a structure predictor, so the quality of that model limits the design.

Most of the fine-tuning data is predicted, not experimental: the OAS stage uses ABodyBuilder2 models that contain no antigen, so antigen context enters only in the smaller SAbDab stage of 1701 clusters.
There is no AbMPNN software release and no model card: the deposit is a dataset record with a weights file, so loading it means matching the ProteinMPNN code version yourself.

The paper is a workshop paper (ICML 2023 Workshop on Computational Biology), and its evaluation is computational: sequence recovery, self-consistency RMSD from a structure predictor and physics-based scoring, with no experimental validation reported.

steps.title: Design sequences with the AbMPNN weights
steps.shell:
python protein_mpnn_run.py \
        --path_to_model_weights ../abmpnn_weights \
        --model_name abmpnn \
        --pdb_path ./inputs/PDB_complexes/pdbs/3HTN.pdb \
        --pdb_path_chains "A B" \
        --out_folder ./outputs/abmpnn_example \
        --num_seq_per_target 2 \
        --sampling_temp "0.2" \
        --seed 37 \
        --batch_size 1
steps.explanation: This is the repository's example 3 command with two flags added from the README's flag list so that the AbMPNN file is loaded instead of a bundled ProteinMPNN checkpoint: --path_to_model_weights selects a weights folder and --model_name a model name. The README documents --model_name only with the bundled ProteinMPNN names such as v_48_020, so a human must check how the loader resolves abmpnn.pt before relying on the command. Replace the PDB path and chains with your antibody structure. The sampling temperature 0.2 is the value the paper used for its SAbDab test set; example 3 itself uses 0.1.
steps.source_locator: examples/submit_example_3.sh; ProteinMPNN README.md: input flags; Paper: section 4

outputs: FASTA output in the out_folder with the designed sequences, each carrying a score, a global score, the designed and fixed chains, the model name, the code git hash, the seed, the sampling temperature and a sequence recovery figure.
limitations: These commands were read from the sources and have not been executed by Rewire.

The final command is a composition: the example script it is based on does not select external weights, and the two weight flags come from the README's flag list, so the exact file naming the loader expects was not verified.
No AbMPNN-specific instructions, model card or compatible code version are published, so the weights may need a ProteinMPNN version close to the 2023 release.
Design is stochastic: the number of sequences, the sampling temperature and the seed all change the output.

torchcraft-20261115-model-abmpnn.notes: AbMPNN has no code repository of its own: the authors (Exscientia) published the fine-tuned weights as the Zenodo dataset 10.5281/zenodo.8164693 under CC BY 4.0, to be run with dauparas/ProteinMPNN (MIT). The code licence fact therefore describes ProteinMPNN, not AbMPNN. The run command in the guide is composed from the ProteinMPNN example script plus the two weight-selection flags in its README; no published AbMPNN command exists, so a human should verify the loader accepts --model_name abmpnn against a folder holding abmpnn.pt. The paper is the ICML 2023 Workshop on Computational Biology version (arXiv 2310.19513v1), read from the PDF text layer extracted locally with pdftotext; the PDF itself is kept beside the text in artifacts/paper.pdf. The record reached this database through the TorchCraft paper, which used AbMPNN as a baseline; nothing on this page comes from that paper.

profile.summary: FlowPacker predicts the side-chain conformations of a protein when the sequence and the backbone coordinates are already known, a task called side-chain packing. It treats the four chi torsion angles of each residue as the only degrees of freedom and generates them with torsional flow matching over an equivariant graph attention network, then writes out the all-atom structure. Two trained checkpoints are published with the code, along with a confidence model that scores several samples so the best can be chosen. It can also fill in only part of a structure, which the authors call inpainting, and works on multi-chain complexes although it was trained on single chains.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract and Introduction; README.md: Inference

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The model is built on the Equiformerv2 architecture with maximum degree 3, channel dimension 256 and 4 blocks, giving 18.0M trainable parameters. Node features are the amino acid identity, the backbone torsion angles and a timestep embedding; the chi angles are produced by flow matching on the torus rather than in Cartesian space, which keeps the side-chain geometry valid by construction. The authors report no gain from raising the maximum degree to 6, and no gain from higher-order solvers such as Heun or RK45 over the plain solver, which cost more runtime. A separate confidence model of 2.2M parameters, trained to regress residue-level side-chain RMSD, is used to pick the best of several samples: unless stated otherwise the authors generate four samples per test case and keep the one with the lowest predicted RMSD.
sections.source_locator: Paper: sections 2.3.2, 2.3.6 and 2.3.7, and Figure 2 caption

sections.title: What it was trained on
sections.body: Two training sets were used, each giving one published checkpoint. BC40 is a set of representative PDB structures clustered at 40 per cent sequence identity, released on 28 July 2020 and used by earlier work; after filtering it gives 36 451 training examples. PDB-S40 is a PDB snapshot clustered the same way, giving 23 191 clusters containing 309 467 structures. Filtering removes structures with more than a quarter of residues unknown, residues with missing backbone coordinates or overlapping alpha carbons, and proteins shorter than 40 residues. The test set is 99 structures: 20 from CASP13, 34 from CASP14 and 45 from CASP15. The authors report that the larger PDB-S40 data improves most metrics over BC40, and the README recommends the cluster.pth checkpoint for most cases.
sections.source_locator: Paper: section 2.3.1 and Results; README.md: checkpoints paragraph

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository holds three checkpoints: bc40.pth, cluster.pth and a confidence model checkpoint, which is switched on or off by setting its path in the config file. The README says checkpoints with other ablations can be provided on request, so only these are public. A result should name the checkpoint, whether confidence sampling was on, how many samples were drawn, and the commit; this page read commit 03421c7fdda73862994aa54fb3077f3f6561408c. Two run options change the output: by default the model masks according to coordinates missing from the input PDB, which suits benchmarking, while the use_gt_masks flag generates all chi angles regardless. The README also warns that its preprocessing may cause minor differences from the input structure.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Inference and checkpoints paragraphs

facts.label: Model type
facts.value: Generative side-chain packing model: torsional flow matching over an equivariant graph attention network, conditioned on sequence and backbone.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Abstract and Introduction

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: Equiformerv2 with maximum degree 3, channel dimension 256 and 4 blocks. Node features: amino acid identity, backbone torsion angles and timestep embedding. A separate confidence model uses maximum degree 2 and hidden dimension 64.
facts.source_locator: Paper: sections 2.3.2 and 2.3.7

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: PDB files holding the sequence and backbone coordinates, read in batch from the folder named by test_path in the inference config. Residues to redesign can be listed with the inpaint flag, using 1-based inclusive ranges per chain.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Inference

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: Predicted side-chain conformations, that is the chi torsion angles and the resulting all-atom coordinates, for the residues being packed; with confidence sampling, the sample with the lowest predicted side-chain RMSD out of those generated. The samples land in ./samples/<name>/, with the confidence-selected structures in best_run and the run metrics in output_dict.pkl.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Abstract and section 2.3.7; README.md: Inference

facts.label: Parameters
facts.value: 18.0M trainable parameters for the packing model, plus 2.2M for the confidence model. Both figures are the authors' own.
facts.source_locator: Paper: sections 2.3.2 and 2.3.7

facts.label: Training data
facts.value: BC40 (representative PDB structures clustered at 40 per cent identity, released 28 July 2020): 36 451 training examples. PDB-S40 (a PDB snapshot clustered at 40 per cent identity): 23 191 clusters containing 309 467 structures. Both are single-chain proteins.
facts.source_locator: Paper: section 2.3.1 and Results

facts.label: Known versions
facts.value: Two packing checkpoints, bc40.pth and cluster.pth (PDB-S40), plus a confidence model checkpoint, all in the repository. Other ablation checkpoints are available on request only. This page read commit 03421c7fdda73862994aa54fb3077f3f6561408c, dated 12 February 2025.
facts.source_locator: README.md: checkpoints paragraphs

facts.label: Training cutoff
facts.value: BC40 carries a release date of 28 July 2020. For PDB-S40 the paper gives no snapshot date; the only related date is the antibody test set filter, which keeps SAbDab structures released after 1 January 2021.
facts.source_locator: Paper: sections 2.3.1 and Results

facts.label: Context limits
facts.value: No fixed limit, but memory bound: the README reports testing on an RTX3060 with 12 GB of VRAM up to 1000 residues, and says extremely long proteins or complexes cause GPU memory problems.

strengths.text: The model is small, 18.0M parameters, and the authors report better runtime than the baselines they compared against, which is their own claim.
Part of a structure can be packed and the rest left alone: the inpaint flag takes residue ranges per chain, which the authors say is not readily available in other packing methods.
Both the code and the two trained checkpoints are in the repository under MIT, with no gate or request step.
The authors report that it transfers to antibody-antigen complexes, with improvements on CDR-H3 and the full variable domain, despite being trained on single chains.

limitations.text: It needs a backbone: the model predicts side chains for a supplied sequence and backbone, so it cannot produce a structure on its own.

Inputs must be cleaned first. The README says unknown or nonstandard amino acids are ignored, overlapping alpha carbons are dropped, and its own preprocessing can introduce minor differences from the input structure.

Long chains run out of GPU memory: the README's tested limit is about 1000 residues on a 12 GB card, and inference is batch-only over a folder, with single-file runs done by putting one PDB in a folder alone.
The model was trained on single-chain proteins, so multimeric and antibody-antigen use is transfer beyond the training distribution, as the authors state themselves.

run_guide.summary: Install the dependencies, put the structures to pack in the folder named by the inference config, and run the sampler to generate side chains.
prerequisites: Python with pip, and torch and torch_geometric builds matching the local CUDA version, installed as the README instructs.
The other packages in requirements.txt, including e3nn, biotite, biopython and numpy 1.22.4.
A GPU: the README reports testing on an RTX3060 with 12 GB of VRAM up to 1000 residues.
PDB files holding sequence and backbone, free of nonstandard residues and overlapping alpha carbons.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit
steps.shell:
git clone https://gitlab.com/mjslee0921/flowpacker.git
cd flowpacker
git checkout --detach 03421c7fdda73862994aa54fb3077f3f6561408c
steps.explanation: The README gives no clone command, so the clone and the checkout of the commit this page read were added here. The checkpoints bc40.pth and cluster.pth come with the repository.
steps.source_locator: README.md: opening lines and checkpoints paragraph

steps.title: Install the environment
steps.shell: pip install -r requirements.txt
steps.explanation: The README's install command. It adds that the appropriate torch and torch_geometric packages should be installed for the local CUDA version, which requirements.txt lists without versions.

steps.title: Point the config at your structures
steps.shell:
mkdir -p my_pdbs
cp /path/to/structure.pdb my_pdbs/
# then set test_path: my_pdbs in ./config/inference/base.yaml
steps.explanation: Inference reads every PDB file in the folder named by test_path in the inference config, so a single structure is run by putting it in a folder on its own. The directory commands here are added; the config setting is the README's.

steps.title: Run the sampler
steps.shell: python sampler_pdb.py base my_run
steps.explanation: The README's inference command: base names the config and the second argument is any label for the run. Add --use_gt_masks True to generate all chi angles regardless of what is missing in the input, or --inpaint A_10-25/B_40/C to pack only those residues and keep the rest native.

outputs: Packed structures written to ./samples/<run name>/, with the confidence-selected structures in best_run.

After sampling, output_dict.pkl holds all the metrics for the inference run. With a confidence checkpoint set in the config, the selected sample is the one with the lowest predicted side-chain RMSD, and --save_traj keeps the whole sampling trajectory.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository and have not been executed by Rewire.
The config file was not fetched, so the default test_path, sample count and confidence setting are unknown; the config must be edited before the run.
Inference is batch-only over a folder, and the README reports GPU memory limits beyond roughly 1000 residues on a 12 GB card.
Generation is stochastic, so repeated runs give different side-chain conformations.

torchcraft-20261115-model-flowpacker.notes: The code is on GitLab, not GitHub, so the commit was taken from the GitLab API (03421c7f, dated 12 February 2025) and the files were fetched from the GitLab raw endpoint at that commit. The 18.0M parameter figure is the paper's for the architecture it describes and is recorded for both packing checkpoints, which share that architecture; the paper does not give per-checkpoint counts. The GitLab project reports no licence in its API metadata, but the repository holds an MIT LICENSE file, which is what the licence facts rest on, and it covers the checkpoints held in the same repository. The paper is open access under CC BY, so its text is stored. The record reached this database through the TorchCraft paper, which used FlowPacker; nothing on this page comes from that paper.
